chapter_note.about: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters. Bottom-up, it starts with every point alone and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, recording each merge in a dendrogram. This chapter covers the bottom-up and top-down views, distances and the closest pair, single, complete and average linkage, reading and cutting a dendrogram, and the chaining effect with its link to the minimum spanning tree.

chapter_note.simple: Hierarchical clustering builds a family tree of your data. Every point starts alone. Then the two closest groups join, again and again, until there is one big group. How you measure the distance between two groups is called the linkage: the nearest pair (single), the farthest pair (complete) or the average of all pairs. Single linkage can make long snakes, and complete linkage makes tight blobs. To get actual clusters, cut the tree with a horizontal line, and count the branches it crosses. In the exam you work from a small table of distances and update it after each merge.

cards.title: Agglomerative versus divisive
cards.simple: Think of a class photo. Agglomerative clustering starts with every student standing alone. Then it keeps joining the two closest groups until everyone is in one big group. Divisive clustering does the opposite: it starts with the whole class together and keeps splitting it. Bottom-up is the version you meet in exams. With n students it needs exactly n − 1 joins, because every join turns two groups into one. The record of who joined whom, and how far apart they were, is called a dendrogram. In exam words: agglomerative clustering is bottom-up with n − 1 merges, and divisive clustering is top-down.
cards.idea: **Agglomerative** clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly **merges** the two closest clusters. Every merge turns two clusters into one, so n points need exactly **n − 1** merges. **Divisive** clustering works top-down: it starts with one cluster and splits. The merge order is recorded as a tree called a **dendrogram**.
cards.definition:
$$\text{clusters left after } m \text{ merges}=n-m,\qquad \text{merges to reach one cluster}=n-1$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of points and $m$ is the number of merges done so far. Bottom-up clustering needs no $k$ in advance: you read the clusters off the finished tree by cutting it.
cards.intuition_full: Counting is the easy part. At the start there are n clusters. A merge takes two clusters and puts them into one, so the count drops by exactly 1. To go from n clusters to 1 you need n − 1 drops, so n − 1 merges. After m merges there are n − m clusters. Divisive clustering runs the film backwards: one cluster at the start and n single points at the end, so a complete run makes n − 1 splits. Unlike k-means, hierarchical clustering needs no starting centroids, so the same data and the same linkage always give the same tree. It needs the full table of pairwise distances, which has about n²/2 entries, so it is slow for very large data. 'Closest clusters' needs a rule for the distance between two groups of points. The linkage cards give three: single, complete and average. For now, the distance between two clusters is the gap between their nearest points.

examples.setup: Six points on a line at A = 0, B = 1, C = 3, D = 7, E = 14, F = 17. Merge bottom-up, always joining the two clusters whose nearest points are closest. List the merges, the height (the gap) of each, and the number of clusters left after each merge.
steps: Start: six single-point clusters. The gaps between neighbours are AB 1, BC 2, CD 4, DE 7, EF 3.
Merge 1: the smallest gap is A–B = 1. Merge them at height 1. Five clusters are left.
Merge 2: B to C is 2, now the smallest gap. C joins {A,B} at height 2. Four clusters are left.
Merge 3: E and F are 3 apart, the smallest gap now. Merge them at height 3. Three clusters are left.
Merge 4: C to D is 4. D joins {A,B,C} at height 4. Two clusters are left.
Merge 5: D to E is 7. The clusters {A,B,C,D} and {E,F} merge at height 7. One cluster is left, after 5 = 6 − 1 merges.

examples.setup: Bottom-up clustering is run on 40 points and stopped when 6 clusters remain. How many merges were made? How many clusters remain after 25 merges? How many merges does the complete tree need?
steps: Each merge removes one cluster. Going from 40 clusters to 6 removes 40 − 6 = 34 clusters, so 34 merges.
After 25 merges: 40 − 25 = 15 clusters.
The complete tree ends with 1 cluster: 40 − 1 = 39 merges.
examples.answer: 34 merges to reach 6 clusters, 15 clusters after 25 merges, 39 merges in all.

examples.setup: Top-down (divisive) clustering is run on 10 points and stopped when 4 clusters exist. How many splits were made? How many merges would bottom-up clustering need to reach 4 clusters from the same 10 points?
steps: Divisive clustering starts with 1 cluster, and each split adds one cluster.
To reach 4 clusters: 4 − 1 = 3 splits.
Bottom-up starts with 10 clusters and each merge removes one. To reach 4 clusters: 10 − 4 = 6 merges.
Check: 3 + 6 = 9 = 10 − 1, the size of the whole tree.
examples.answer: 3 splits top-down, 6 merges bottom-up. They add up to n − 1 = 9.

cards.title: Distances and the closest pair
cards.simple: To decide who is closest, you first need a ruler. Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance, like a crow flying. Manhattan distance is the walking distance along a city grid: first across, then up. The two rulers can disagree about which pair is closest. Once you pick a ruler, write all the pair distances in a table. This is the distance matrix. The first merge is the smallest number in the table, ignoring the diagonal, because the diagonal is each point's distance to itself, which is zero. In exam words: compute the pairwise distances (L1 or L2), then merge the smallest off-diagonal entry.
cards.idea: Before merging you need a **distance** between points. **Euclidean** (L2) is the straight-line distance. **Manhattan** (L1) adds the gaps in each coordinate. Write all pair distances in a symmetric **distance matrix**, then merge the pair with the smallest **off-diagonal** entry. The diagonal is always 0 and means nothing.
cards.definition:
$$d_2(p,q)=\sqrt{\sum_i (p_i-q_i)^2},\qquad d_1(p,q)=\sum_i |p_i-q_i|$$

Symbols: $p$ and $q$ are two points and $p_i$ is coordinate $i$. The distance matrix has $d(p,q)$ in row $p$ and column $q$. It is symmetric and its diagonal is 0. For $n$ points there are $n(n-1)/2$ different pairs.
cards.intuition_full: Euclidean distance is the length of the straight line between two points. Manhattan distance is the length of a path that moves only along the axes, like a taxi in a city grid: add the gap in each coordinate. For two points that differ by (3, 4), the straight line is 5 but the taxi route is 7. Because the two rulers measure differently, they can disagree about which pair is closest, and then the first merge differs. Read the question for the metric. Next, build the table of all pairs. It is symmetric, because the distance from A to B equals the distance from B to A, so you only need half of it. Its diagonal is 0 because each point is at distance 0 from itself, and those zeros are never a candidate for a merge. Merge the smallest off-diagonal number. For 4 points there are 6 pairs, for 5 points 10 pairs, and n(n − 1)/2 in general.

examples.setup: Four points in the plane: P = (0, 0), Q = (3, 4), R = (8, 0), S = (14, 0). Find the closest pair under the Manhattan distance and under the Euclidean distance.
steps: Four points, six pairs. Compute each pair under both rulers.
P–Q: the gaps are 3 and 4. Manhattan = 3 + 4 = 7. Euclidean = √(9 + 16) = 5.
R–S: the gaps are 6 and 0. Manhattan = 6 and Euclidean = 6.
The other pairs. Manhattan: P–R 8, Q–R 9, P–S 14, Q–S 15. Euclidean: P–R 8, Q–R √41 = 6.4, P–S 14, Q–S √137 = 11.7.
Smallest Manhattan distance: R–S = 6 (then P–Q = 7). Smallest Euclidean distance: P–Q = 5 (then R–S = 6).
examples.answer: Manhattan: R and S merge first, at 6. Euclidean: P and Q merge first, at 5.

examples.setup: Four points in 3-D: P1 = (0, 1, −3), P2 = (0, 4, −1), P3 = (0, 4, 3), P4 = (−3, 1, 3). Hierarchical clustering uses the Manhattan distance. Which pair merges first, and at what distance?
steps: The smallest of the six is 4, for P2 and P3.
Under the Euclidean distance P1–P2 would win instead, with √13 ≈ 3.6 against √16 = 4 for P2–P3.
examples.answer: P2 and P3 merge first, at distance 4.

examples.setup: Four objects A, B, C, D have these distances: AB 2, AC 5, AD 6, BC 4, BD 7, CD 2. Two entries tie for the smallest. Which pair merges first, and does it matter? What is the single-linkage distance between the two new clusters?
steps: The smallest entry is 2, and it appears twice: A–B and C–D.
The two pairs share no point, so both merge at height 2, in either order.
The two new clusters are {A,B} and {C,D}. Their single-linkage distance is the smallest cross pair: min(AC 5, AD 6, BC 4, BD 7) = 4.
examples.answer: Both merge at height 2, and the order does not matter. The next merge is at 4.

cards.why: The first merge depends on the metric and the table, and a wrong first merge spoils every step after it. In GATE: compute pairwise Manhattan or Euclidean distances and find the first merge.
how: Use the metric the question names (L1 or L2).
Compute the distance for every pair, n(n − 1)/2 of them.
Write them in a symmetric table and ignore the zero diagonal.
The smallest off-diagonal entry is the first merge.
With Euclidean distance, compare squared values to avoid roots.
cards.mistake: Taking a diagonal zero as the closest pair, or using Euclidean distance when the question says Manhattan. The diagonal compares a point with itself. Use the named metric on every pair.
edge_cases: Squared Euclidean distances rank pairs the same way as Euclidean ones, so skip the root when you only compare.
Manhattan is never smaller than Euclidean. They are equal when only one coordinate differs.
A tie for the smallest entry: when the pairs do not overlap, both merge at that height.
In three dimensions, add a third gap term.
connections: Foundations: Algebra. Absolute values, squares and square roots.
k-NN uses the same two distances to find neighbours.
k-means uses squared Euclidean distance. Hierarchical clustering lets you choose the metric.

cards.title: Single linkage
cards.simple: Single linkage measures how far apart two groups are by their two closest members, like judging two villages by their nearest houses. One friendly pair is enough to call two groups close. At each step you join the two groups with the smallest such gap. In the table, the new group's row is just the smaller of the two old rows. Because one close pair is enough, a trail of close points can join into one long snake. In exam words: single linkage uses the minimum distance over cross pairs, d(A, B) = min d(a, b).
cards.idea: In **single linkage** the distance between two clusters is the **smallest** distance between a point in one and a point in the other. At each step, merge the two clusters with the smallest such distance. After a merge, the new cluster's distance to any other cluster is the **minimum** of the two old distances.
cards.definition:
$$d(A,B)=\min_{a\in A,\ b\in B}d(a,b),\qquad d(K,\,I\cup J)=\min\bigl(d(K,I),\,d(K,J)\bigr)$$

Symbols: $A$, $B$, $K$, $I$, $J$ are clusters and $d(a,b)$ is the distance between two points. The second formula updates the table after clusters $I$ and $J$ merge: the new row is the smaller of the two old rows.
cards.intuition_full: One close pair is enough. If a point is near any member of a cluster, single linkage treats the whole cluster as near. That makes the update rule easy: the distance from a third cluster K to the merged cluster is the smaller of its distances to the two parts, because the closest pair runs through one part or the other. So you never need the original table again. Just take the element-wise minimum of the two rows. The merge heights never go down. The price is chaining: a path of close points can pull far-apart points into one cluster, as the twist example shows.

examples.setup: Five points A to E with these distances: AB 3, AC 8, AD 8, AE 10, BC 5, BD 2, BE 9, CD 12, CE 6, DE 4. Run single linkage and give the merge heights.
steps: Five single-point clusters. The smallest entry in the table is B–D = 2.
Merge {B, D} at height 2. New distances by the min rule: A: min(3, 8) = 3. C: min(5, 12) = 5. E: min(9, 4) = 4.
The smallest entry is now A to {B,D} = 3. Merge {A,B,D} at height 3. New distances: C: min(8, 5, 12) = 5. E: min(10, 9, 4) = 4.
The smallest is E to {A,B,D} = 4. Merge {A,B,D,E} at height 4. C to that cluster: min(8, 5, 12, 6) = 5.
C joins last at height 5. The heights are 2, 3, 4, 5.
examples.answer: Merges: {B,D} at 2, then A at 3, then E at 4, then C at 5. The tree is a chain.

examples.setup: Single linkage on five points with these distances: P1P2 2, P1P3 6, P1P4 7, P1P5 9, P2P3 4, P2P4 3, P2P5 4, P3P4 8, P3P5 5, P4P5 2. Give the merge heights in order, and the clusters when the dendrogram is cut at 3.5.
steps: Two entries tie for the smallest: P1–P2 = 2 and P4–P5 = 2. The pairs do not overlap, so both merge at height 2.
Compare {P1,P2} with {P4,P5}: min(P1P4 7, P1P5 9, P2P4 3, P2P5 4) = 3. P3 to {P1,P2}: min(6, 4) = 4. P3 to {P4,P5}: min(8, 5) = 5.
The smallest is 3: merge {P1,P2} and {P4,P5} at height 3.
Last, P3 to the other four: min(6, 4, 8, 5) = 4. Merge at height 4.
Heights 2, 2, 3, 4. Cut at 3.5: keep the merges at 3 or lower. The clusters are {P1,P2,P4,P5} and {P3}.
examples.answer: Heights 2, 2, 3, 4. The cut at 3.5 gives 2 clusters: {P1,P2,P4,P5} and {P3}.

examples.setup: Use the five-point table of the basic example. The points A and E are far apart: A–E = 10. At what height do A and E end up in the same cluster under single linkage?
steps: A and E meet when E joins the cluster {A,B,D}.
E to {A,B,D} = min(A–E 10, B–E 9, D–E 4) = 4.
The pair D–E is close (4) and D is already inside the cluster, so E joins at height 4.
The distance A–E = 10 never mattered.
examples.answer: At height 4, although A and E are 10 apart. One close pair is enough. That is chaining.

cards.why: Single linkage is the linkage GATE has asked you to run. In GATE: run it on a distance matrix and choose the right dendrogram, or state that it uses the minimum.
how: Find the smallest off-diagonal entry and merge those two clusters at that height.
Rewrite the table: the new cluster's distance to each other cluster is the min of the two old distances.
Repeat on the smaller table.
Record each height. They never decrease.
Read the tree, or cut it as the question asks.
cards.mistake: Swapping min and max (single is min, complete is max), or averaging the old entries. For single linkage keep the smaller of the two old distances, not the mean and not the larger one.
edge_cases: Tied smallest entries: if the pairs do not overlap, merge both at that height. If they overlap, the tree shape can change but the heights stay the same.
Merge heights are non-decreasing.
With two clusters left, the last height is their single-linkage distance.
Single-linkage heights equal the minimum spanning tree edge weights (see the last card).
connections: Foundations: Algebra. Taking the smaller of two numbers.
Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal's algorithm gives the same heights.
Complete and average linkage cards: the same table with a different update rule.

cards.title: Complete linkage
cards.simple: Complete linkage measures how far apart two groups are by their two farthest members, like saying two villages are close only if every house in one is near every house in the other. So it is hard to call two groups close. At each step you join the two groups with the smallest such worst-case gap. In the table, the new group's row takes the larger of the two old entries. This builds tight, round groups, because nobody in a cluster can be far from anybody else. In exam words: complete linkage uses the maximum distance over cross pairs, d(A, B) = max d(a, b).
cards.idea: In **complete linkage** the distance between two clusters is the **largest** distance between a point in one and a point in the other. After a merge, the new cluster's distance to any other cluster is the **maximum** of the two old distances. The result is compact clusters: every pair inside a cluster is within the merge height.
cards.definition:
$$d(A,B)=\max_{a\in A,\ b\in B}d(a,b),\qquad d(K,\,I\cup J)=\max\bigl(d(K,I),\,d(K,J)\bigr)$$

Symbols: the same as for single linkage. The second formula updates the table after $I$ and $J$ merge: the new row is the larger of the two old rows.
cards.intuition_full: Complete linkage asks for the worst case: two clusters are close only if even their farthest members are close. So a cluster can only grow if the newcomer is near everyone already inside. That keeps clusters tight: when two clusters merge at height h, every pair of points in the merged cluster is at distance at most h. This is the opposite of single linkage, where one close pair is enough. The price is sensitivity to outliers, because one far point inflates all the distances to its cluster, and the method may split a long, thin natural group. The update rule mirrors single linkage: the element-wise maximum of the two old rows.

cards.title: Average linkage
cards.simple: Average linkage measures how far apart two groups are by looking at every pair with one member in each group and taking the typical distance. It is a fair middle path: not just the nearest pair, and not just the farthest. If group X has 2 people and group Y has 3, there are 6 cross pairs. Add the 6 distances and divide by 6. When groups were already merged, do not just average the old averages: bigger groups count for more. In exam words: average linkage is the mean of all |A|·|B| cross-pair distances, and the update weights the old distances by cluster size.
cards.idea: In **average linkage** the distance between two clusters is the **mean** of all cross-pair distances: add up the |A| × |B| distances between a point of A and a point of B, and divide by |A||B|. The value always lies between the single (min) and the complete (max) value. When you update, weight the old averages by the **cluster sizes**.
cards.definition:
$$d(A,B)=\frac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b),\qquad d(K,\,I\cup J)=\frac{|I|\,d(K,I)+|J|\,d(K,J)}{|I|+|J|}$$

Symbols: $|A|$ is the number of points in cluster $A$. The double sum runs over every pair with one point in each cluster. The second formula is the size-weighted update after $I$ and $J$ merge.
cards.intuition_full: A mean over all cross distances is a balanced judgement. One outlier no longer decides, as it does in complete linkage, and one near pair no longer decides, as it does in single linkage. The cost is bookkeeping. You can always go back to the original table and average every cross pair. That is slow but certain. Or you can use the update rule, which gives the same answer: the distance from K to the merged cluster is the size-weighted average of the two old distances. The weights matter. If I has two points and J has one, the answer is 2/3 of d(K, I) plus 1/3 of d(K, J), not a half-and-half mix. The first merge is the same for every linkage, because singletons have only one pair.

cards.title: Dendrogram and cuts
cards.simple: A dendrogram is a family tree of the merges. The people (points) stand along the bottom. Each time two groups join, a horizontal bar connects them, and the height of the bar tells you how far apart the groups were when they joined. To get actual groups, cut the tree with a horizontal line at some height. Groups that joined below the line stay together, and everything that joins above the line is kept apart. Count the branches the line crosses to get the number of groups. A long stretch of the tree with no joins is a good place to cut. In exam words: the height is the merge distance, and a cut at h keeps the merges at or below h.
cards.idea: A **dendrogram** draws the merges as a tree. Each bar sits at the **height** equal to the distance of that merge. A horizontal **cut** at height h keeps the merges at or below h, and the branches the line crosses are the clusters. After m kept merges there are n − m clusters.
cards.definition:
$$\text{clusters at cut }h \;=\; n-\#\{\text{merges with height}\le h\}$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of points. A merge is kept if its height is at most $h$. For single, complete and average linkage the heights never decrease, so the kept merges are the lowest ones.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the tree as a record played from the bottom up. Each bar says: at this distance, these two groups joined. Lower bars joined earlier because their groups were closer. Placing a horizontal line at height h freezes the film at distance h: everything that had joined by then is one cluster, and everything else is still separate. The number of branches crossing the line is the number of clusters. Because every merge reduces the cluster count by one, you can also count: n minus the number of bars below the line. A long vertical stretch with no bars means that the clusters stay the same over a wide range of cut heights, so that number of clusters is robust. A short stretch means the number of clusters is fragile. Remember that height is a distance, not a merge number, and the left-to-right order of leaves can be flipped without changing the tree.

examples.setup: Complete linkage on the five-point table gave merges {B,D} at 2, {C,E} at 6, A joining {B,D} at 8, and the last merge at 12. Draw the tree, cut it at h = 7 and at h = 10, and say where a cut is most stable.
steps: Leaves at the bottom. Each merge is a bar at its distance: B,D at 2, C,E at 6, A joins at 8, the last at 12.
The height of a bar is the distance of that merge. It is not the number of the merge.
Cut at h = 7: the bars at 2 and 6 are kept, so 5 − 2 = 3 clusters: {A}, {B,D}, {C,E}. The line crosses three branches.
Cut at h = 10: the bars at 2, 6 and 8 are kept, so 5 − 3 = 2 clusters: {A,B,D} and {C,E}.
Any cut between 8 and 12 gives the same two clusters, a stretch of 4. Three clusters hold only between 6 and 8, a stretch of 2.
examples.answer: A cut at 7 gives 3 clusters and a cut at 10 gives 2 clusters. Two clusters is the more stable choice.

examples.setup: A dendrogram on six points has merge heights 1, 2, 4, 9 and 10. How many clusters does a cut at h = 5 give? For which cut heights do you get exactly 2 clusters, and how long is that stretch? Which number of clusters has the widest stretch?
steps: Cut at 5: the merges with height at most 5 are 1, 2 and 4, so 3 merges. Clusters = 6 − 3 = 3.
Exactly 2 clusters needs 4 merges kept: 1, 2, 4, 9 are kept and 10 is not. That means 9 ≤ h < 10, a stretch of length 1.
Exactly 3 clusters: 4 ≤ h < 9, a stretch of length 5. Exactly 4 clusters: 2 ≤ h < 4, length 2.
The widest stretch is for 3 clusters.
examples.answer: A cut at 5 gives 3 clusters. Exactly 2 clusters need 9 ≤ h < 10 (length 1). The widest stretch (length 5) gives 3 clusters.

examples.setup: A dendrogram on 8 points has merge heights 1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9. How many clusters does a cut at h = 6.5 give?
steps: Merges with height at most 6.5: 1, 2, 2, 3 and 6. That is 5 merges.
Clusters = 8 − 5 = 3.
A common slip is to answer 5, the number of merges. The number of clusters is what is left.
examples.answer: 3 clusters.

A **dendrogram** draws the merges as a tree. Each bar sits at the **height** equal to the distance of that merge. A horizontal **cut** at height h keeps the merges at or below h, and the branches the line crosses are the clusters. After m kept merges there are n − m clusters.

$$\text{clusters at cut }h \;=\; n-\#\{\text{merges with height}\le h\}$$

Symbols: $n$ is the number of points. A merge is kept if its height is at most $h$. For single, complete and average linkage the heights never decrease, so the kept merges are the lowest ones.

**Worked example.** Complete linkage on the five-point table gave merges {B,D} at 2, {C,E} at 6, A joining {B,D} at 8, and the last merge at 12. Draw the tree, cut it at h = 7 and at h = 10, and say where a cut is most stable.

1. Leaves at the bottom. Each merge is a bar at its distance: B,D at 2, C,E at 6, A joins at 8, the last at 12.
2. The height of a bar is the distance of that merge. It is not the number of the merge.
3. Cut at h = 7: the bars at 2 and 6 are kept, so 5 − 2 = 3 clusters: {A}, {B,D}, {C,E}. The line crosses three branches.
4. Cut at h = 10: the bars at 2, 6 and 8 are kept, so 5 − 3 = 2 clusters: {A,B,D} and {C,E}.
5. Any cut between 8 and 12 gives the same two clusters, a stretch of 4. Three clusters hold only between 6 and 8, a stretch of 2.

**Answer:** A cut at 7 gives 3 clusters and a cut at 10 gives 2 clusters. Two clusters is the more stable choice.

**Check yourself:** A dendrogram on 7 points has heights 1, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9. How many clusters at h = 4?

*Answer:* Merges at or below 4: 1, 3, 3, so 3 merges. 7 − 3 = 4 clusters.
cards.trap: Reading the height as the order of merging, or counting merges instead of clusters. The height is the distance. After m kept merges there are n − m clusters.
cards.why_full:
Reading a dendrogram is how hierarchical clustering gives you clusters. In GATE: pick the dendrogram that matches a merge sequence, or count the clusters at a cut.

cards.title: Chaining and the MST link
cards.simple: Single linkage is like making friends through friends. If I know someone who knows someone, we end up in the same group, even if you and I have nothing in common. A string of close points can link two far-away groups into one long snake. That is chaining. Complete linkage is stricter: you join a group only if you are close to everybody in it, so groups stay compact. There is also a neat fact. The heights of the single-linkage tree are exactly the edge lengths of the minimum spanning tree, which is the cheapest set of links that connects every point. In exam words: single linkage chains, complete linkage gives compact clusters, and single-linkage merge heights equal the MST edge weights.
cards.idea: **Single linkage chains**: one close pair is enough to join clusters, so a path of close points becomes one long cluster. **Complete linkage** needs every pair to be close, so its clusters stay **compact**. The merge heights of single linkage are exactly the edge weights of the **minimum spanning tree**.
cards.definition:
$$\{\text{single-linkage heights}\}\;=\;\{\text{edge weights of a minimum spanning tree}\}$$

Symbols: the minimum spanning tree (MST) of the points is the cheapest set of $n-1$ edges that connects all of them, found by Kruskal's algorithm: sort the edges by weight and add each one unless it closes a cycle. The weights, in sorted order, are the single-linkage merge heights.
cards.intuition_full: Kruskal's algorithm and single linkage are the same procedure in two costumes. Kruskal takes the cheapest remaining edge that joins two different components. Single linkage takes the closest pair of clusters, and the closest pair of clusters is exactly the cheapest edge between two different components. So the edges Kruskal picks, in order, have the same weights as the single-linkage heights. That also explains chaining. The MST only needs a chain of short edges to connect distant points, and single linkage follows that chain. Complete linkage looks at the farthest pair instead, so it cannot be fooled by a chain: it needs every pair in a cluster to be within the merge height. The cost is the opposite weakness: one far outlier inflates all distances to its cluster.

how: Single linkage: one close pair joins clusters, so look for chains.
Complete linkage: every pair must be close, so clusters are compact.
MST link: single-linkage heights equal the MST edge weights, in increasing order.
To total the heights, run Kruskal: sort the edges and skip any that close a cycle.
State the weaknesses: chaining for single, outlier sensitivity for complete.
cards.mistake: Saying chaining is a weakness of complete linkage, or that single linkage gives compact clusters. Chaining belongs to single linkage. Complete linkage gives compact clusters.
edge_cases: Chaining can be useful: single linkage follows long, thin or curved shapes that complete linkage would cut into pieces.
Complete linkage is sensitive to outliers.
Average linkage sits between the two.
The MST link holds for single linkage only.
connections: Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal's algorithm produces the same weights as single linkage.
k-means: its clusters are convex, like the compact clusters of complete linkage.
Foundations: Algebra. Sorting and adding a short list of numbers.

scenes.title: Bottom-up: n points need n − 1 merges

steps.caption: Six points on a line at A = 0, B = 1, C = 3, D = 7, E = 14, F = 17. Bottom-up clustering starts with six clusters, one per point.
Merge 1: the closest two clusters are A and B, 1 apart. Merge them at height 1. Five clusters are left.
Merge 2: B to C is 2, the smallest gap now. C joins {A,B} at height 2. Four clusters are left.
Merge 3: E and F are 3 apart, the smallest gap now. Merge them at height 3. Three clusters are left.
Merge 4: C to D is 4. D joins {A,B,C} at height 4. Two clusters are left.
Merge 5: D to E is 7. The two clusters {A,B,C,D} and {E,F} merge at height 7. One cluster is left, after 5 = 6 − 1 merges.

scenes.title: Manhattan and Euclidean distance can disagree

steps.caption: Four points in the plane: P = (0, 0), Q = (3, 4), R = (8, 0) and S = (14, 0). Which pair do we merge first? It depends on the ruler.
P to Q: the gaps are 3 across and 4 up. Manhattan distance adds the gaps: 3 + 4 = 7 (the dashed path). Euclidean distance is the straight line: √(9 + 16) = 5.
R to S: the gaps are 6 across and 0 up. Manhattan = 6 and Euclidean = 6. The two rulers agree here.
The other four pairs are larger. Manhattan: P–R 8, Q–R 9, P–S 14, Q–S 15. Euclidean: P–R 8, Q–R 6.4, P–S 14, Q–S 11.7.
Smallest Manhattan distance: R–S = 6, against P–Q = 7. Smallest Euclidean distance: P–Q = 5, against R–S = 6. Different rulers merge different pairs first.

scenes.title: Single linkage on a five-point table

steps.caption: The table of distances for five points (only the upper half is shown). Each point starts as its own cluster. The smallest entry is B to D = 2.
Merge B and D at height 2. A bar at height 2 joins their two lines.
Single linkage: the new distance is the minimum of the old ones. A to {B,D} = min(3, 8) = 3. This is now the smallest entry, so A joins at height 3.
E to {A,B,D} = min(10, 9, 4) = 4. It is the smallest, so E joins at height 4, even though A and E are 10 apart.
C to {A,B,D,E} = min(8, 5, 12, 6) = 5. C joins last, at height 5. The heights are 2, 3, 4, 5: a staircase, a chain.

scenes.title: Complete linkage on the same table

steps.caption: The same table. The smallest entry is B to D = 2, so the first merge is the same as in single linkage.
Merge B and D at height 2.
Complete linkage takes the maximum. A to {B,D} = max(3, 8) = 8, C to {B,D} = 12, E to {B,D} = 9. The smallest entry is now C to E = 6, so C and E merge at height 6.
A to {B,D} = 8 is the smallest, since A to {C,E} = max(8, 10) = 10. A joins {B,D} at height 8, not at 3.
Last merge: {A,B,D} to {C,E} is the largest of the six cross distances 8, 10, 5, 9, 12, 4, which is 12. The heights are 2, 6, 8, 12.

scenes.title: Average linkage on the same table

steps.caption: The same table. The first merge is the smallest entry, B to D = 2, for every linkage.
Merge B and D at height 2.
Average linkage: A to {B,D} = (3 + 8) / 2 = 5.5. The others are larger: C = (5 + 12) / 2 = 8.5, E = (9 + 4) / 2 = 6.5. So A joins at height 5.5.
Now C to {A,B,D} = (8 + 5 + 12) / 3 = 8.33 and E to {A,B,D} = (10 + 9 + 4) / 3 = 7.67. C to E = 6 is smaller than both, so C and E merge at height 6.
Last merge: average of all six cross distances = (8 + 10 + 5 + 9 + 12 + 4) / 6 = 48 / 6 = 8. The heights are 2, 5.5, 6, 8.

The dendrogram of complete linkage on the table of the last cards. Leaves are at the bottom. Each bar is a merge, drawn at the distance where it happened: B,D at 2, C,E at 6, A joins at 8, the last at 12.
The height of a bar is the linkage distance of that merge, not the number of the merge.
Cut at h = 7: keep the merges at 7 or lower, the bars at 2 and 6. The line crosses three branches, so there are three clusters: {A}, {B,D} and {C,E}.
Cut at h = 10: the bars at 2, 6 and 8 are kept. Two branches are crossed, so there are two clusters: {A,B,D} and {C,E}.
A long vertical stretch with no merge means a stable choice. Any cut between 8 and 12 gives the same two clusters, a stretch of 4. Three clusters hold only between 6 and 8, a stretch of 2.
